newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African maize farmers warned not to over-plant.
newsitem.headline: S.African maize farmers warned not to over-plant.

text.p: South Africa's maize producers' organisation Nampo warned farmers to be wary of planting crops on less fertile land to prevent a surplus in the coming season.

National Maize Producers' Organisation chairman Japie Grobler said on Monday night that the organisation could not assure its members that a maize marketing scheme would be in place for the 1997/1998 season (May-April).

"If producers do not succeed this year to negotiate a pre-planting contract of 550 rand a tonne or more for their maize, they should seriously consider only planting maize on their very best land," Grobler said in a statement after a meeting of the Maize Advisory Committee on Monday night.

Grobler said after talks between members of the Advisory Committee -- representing producers, traders and the state's Maize Board -- on Monday it was clear that some players were against stability in the domestic maize industry.
"It is clear that some of the role-players are strongly against stability in the maize industry for their own reasons," Grobler said.
The Maize Board has already said it will be dissolved and withdrawn from the export market by the start of the new season if the industry is able to agree on a future marketing system.

Board general manager Leon du Plessis told Reuters a rough timetable for the closing of the board had been drawn up following new agricultural legislation which requires the dismantling of all control boards.
Although the board withdrew from intervention in the domestic market in 1995, it is still active -- alongside private traders -- in the export market where it fixes a floor price.
Grobler said Nampo could not give any assurances to its members that a floor price system would be in place next season.

"Therefore they have to take decisions about planting very carefully. World prices continue to decrease and it is better for each producer to rather plant less maize than too much and then to sell the maize at massive losses," he said.
"Without a maize (marketing) scheme, all surpluses which are exported would pull down maize prices to very low levels."
The Advisory Committee said on Tuesday that discussions on future maize marketing arrangements from next season would be held at its next meeting on November 22.
South Africa's parliament last month passed the Marketing of Agricultural Products Bill which sets a 13-month timetable for the dismantling of remaining farming control boards .
The bill also compels industries to manage their affairs on a market-related basis.
